h: פָּרָשַׁת שְׁקָלִים, מַאֲמָר י״ד Parshas Shekalim — Maamar Yud Daled

p: from twenty years old and up,
for the counting from age twenty
was only in the time of Moshe Rabbeinu,
And the mitzvah of shekalim applied
and not at a time of counting.
So what is the point of Parshas Shekalim,
of which they said in the Tanchuma (Ki Sisa 3)
שֶׁאָמַר לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לְמֹשֶׁה
that Hakadosh Baruch Hu said to Moshe
that every year that Parshas Shekalim is read
it is as if you are standing
But the matter is as we said:
that at the time of the count,
which shows that each one of Yisrael
is a significant thing before Hashem Yisbarach,
an accusation was aroused over this.
that each one of Yisrael has within him
a special portion of the words of Torah,
and the accuser argues that there are many amei ha'aretz
who have no knowledge at all
to the point that their deliberate sins are counted as inadvertent,
And for this Yisrael needed a blessing
before the count and after it,
as they said in the holy Zohar
(רֵישׁ פָּרָשַׁת כִּי תִשָּׂא חֵלֶק ב קפז, ב)
And the essence of the blessing
is an outpouring in words of Torah.
"And you shall take the atonement money," etc.,
שֶׁעַל יְדֵי שֶׁמֹּשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם
that because Moshe Rabbeinu, alav hashalom,
for the service of the Ohel Moed,
he accomplished for Yisrael for all generations
that they would always merit, through the act of the shekalim,
to bring about, from the root,
of the level of Moshe Rabbeinu, alav hashalom.
that they give the shekalim for the korbanos,
even though they are not being counted,
אָז ה׳ יִתְבָּרַךְ מוֹנֶה אֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל
is a thing that is counted,
which has a special portion in the Torah.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁזִּיכָּה מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם
And just as Moshe Rabbeinu, alav hashalom, granted merit
to Yisrael, as it is written (Devarim 33:4):
an inheritance of the congregation of Yaakov" —
as they said in the Gemara (there) —
גַּם כֵּן יֵשׁ לָהֶם חֵלֶק בַּתּוֹרָה
they too have a portion in the Torah.
And this takes effect even when there is no mizbeach,
which is like the act of the shekalim;
from those counted from age twenty,
שֶׁה׳ יִתְבָּרַךְ מוֹנֶה וּפוֹקֵד אֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל
that Hashem Yisbarach counts and remembers Yisrael,
and one merits a blessing before Him,
an outpouring in words of Torah,
"The blessing of Hashem, it makes rich" —
And there is a blessing after the count,
as at the time of the count
as they said in the holy Zohar (there):
at the beginning and at the end."
And they merit an outpouring in words of Torah,
and Shabbos is the time for this,
that the Torah was given on Shabbos (Shabbos 86b).
this is the Torah she'b'al peh,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (זֹהַר חֵלֶק א מז, ב)

paragraphs.text: Exodus 30:14 — “Everyone who passes among those counted, from twenty years old and upward, shall give the Lord’s contribution.” Rav Tzadok begins with the original census setting, then asks why its language remains central to the annual reading of Shekalim.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Rashi on Bamidbar 1:1 — “Out of their dearness before Him He counts them at every moment: when they left Egypt He counted them, when they fell through the Calf He counted them to know the number of those remaining.” Rashi supplies the premise of Rav Tzadok’s point: being counted is itself a sign of each Jew’s importance before Hashem, which is exactly what arouses the accuser’s challenge.

paragraphs.text: Bava Metzia 33b:2–3 — “What did they expound? As Rabbi Judah son of Rabbi Ilai expounded: What is meant by ‘Declare to My people their transgression, and to the house of Jacob their sin’? ‘Declare to My people their transgression’—these are Torah scholars, whose inadvertent errors are reckoned as intentional sins. ‘And to the house of Jacob their sin’—these are the unlearned, whose intentional sins are reckoned as inadvertent errors. This is what we learned: Rabbi Judah says, Be careful in study, for an error in study is reckoned as an intentional sin.” The distinction concerns responsibility corresponding to knowledge. The same passage supplies Rav Tzadok’s later designation of the unlearned as the house of Jacob.

paragraphs.text: Zohar II 187b, Ki Tisa 1:2–3 — “A blessing from above does not rest on something that has been counted. If you ask, How then were Israel counted? A ransom was taken from them. ... The reckoning did not take place until all that ransom had been gathered, and it entered the count. First they bless Israel; afterward they count that ransom; afterward they return and bless Israel. Thus Israel are blessed at the beginning and at the end, and death does not arise among them. Why does death arise through counting? Because blessing does not rest upon a count. Once blessing has departed, the other side rests upon it and can cause harm. Therefore they take a ransom and redemption, so that the reckoning may fall upon it.” The blessings surround a count of the ransom money, protecting the people whose lives it represents.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Resisei Layla 26 — “Just as there are 600,000 letters in the Torah, every soul of Yisrael has a special portion in the Torah… and the count is called ‘lift the head,’ for each has a particular elevation, since every portion of Torah or the Mishkan is needed, and if one is missing it is invalid.” This explains why Hashem’s counting of each soul signals a portion in Torah that no other Jew can fill.

paragraphs.text: Deuteronomy 33:4 — “Moses commanded us Torah, an inheritance of the congregation of Jacob.” The Torah is the inheritance of the entire congregation. Rav Tzadok includes even those whom the Talmud calls the house of Jacob—the unlearned—in this shared inheritance.

paragraphs.text: Proverbs 10:22 — “The blessing of the Lord—it makes wealthy, and He adds no sorrow with it.” The verse speaks of the wealth of divine blessing; Rav Tzadok applies that wealth here to the individual’s portion in Torah.

paragraphs.text: Tikkunei Zohar, Introduction 17a — “You brought forth ten arrangements, and we call them ten sefirot, through which to direct concealed worlds that are not revealed and worlds that are revealed. ... Malkhut is the mouth: we call it Oral Torah.” The specific formula “Malkhut is the mouth, Oral Torah” is found in the introduction to Tikkunei Zohar, in Patach Eliyahu. It complements the preceding Zohar passage about the seventh day.
